title: How a Robin Builds a Nest
standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions about key details in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A robin needs a safe place to lay her eggs.

paras.label: B
paras.text: She finds a strong fork where a tree branch splits in two.

paras.label: C
paras.text: She brings grass and small twigs to the fork, one piece at a time.

paras.label: D
paras.text: She packs wet mud inside the bowl and presses it down with her chest.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The mud dries hard and holds the whole nest together.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A robin needs a safe place for her eggs.

paras.label: B
paras.text: She finds a fork in a tree branch.

paras.label: C
paras.text: She brings grass and twigs to the fork.

paras.label: D
paras.text: She packs wet mud inside the nest.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The mud dries hard and holds it together.

questions.q: Where does the robin build her nest?
questions.a: She finds a strong fork where a tree branch splits in two.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. grass and twigs) and paragraph D (i.e. the wet mud).
Tell how a robin builds a nest.
questions.a: She finds a fork in a tree branch, brings grass and twigs one piece at a time, packs wet mud inside, and the mud dries hard and holds the nest together.

questions.q:
fork: the place where a branch splits in two.
twig: a very small, thin stick.
Describe the connection between the mud and the nest staying together.
questions.a: She packs wet mud inside the bowl, and the mud dries hard and holds the whole nest together.

note: RI.1.1 is asking and answering from details, so every answer is printed. Have the child put a finger on the sentence before saying it out loud.

title: What a Frog Catches
standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions about key details in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A frog sits very still at the edge of the pond.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It waits for a bug to fly close enough.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A frog's tongue is long, pink and very sticky.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The tongue snaps out and grabs the bug in a flash.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The whole catch takes less than one second to finish.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A frog sits still at the pond.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It waits for a bug to come close.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its tongue is long and sticky.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The tongue snaps out and grabs the bug.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The whole catch is very fast.

questions.q: What is a frog's tongue like?
questions.a: A frog's tongue is long, pink and very sticky.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. waiting) and paragraph D (i.e. the catch).
Tell how a frog catches a bug.
questions.a: It sits very still at the edge of the pond and waits for a bug to come close. Then its long sticky tongue snaps out and grabs the bug in less than one second.

questions.q:
sticky: able to hold on to things that touch it.
snaps: moves out very fast and then back again.
Describe the connection between sitting still and catching a bug.
questions.a: The frog sits very still and waits for a bug to fly close enough, so the bug comes near without being scared away.

note: Paragraph A and paragraph B are both about waiting. Ask why the writer gave waiting two paragraphs when the catch only gets one.

title: The Crossing Guard
standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions about key details in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A crossing guard stands at the corner by the school.

paras.label: B
paras.text: She wears a bright vest so every driver can see her.

paras.label: C
paras.text: She holds up a round sign that tells cars to stop.

paras.label: D
paras.text: When the cars stop, she waves the children across the street.

paras.label: E
paras.text: She stays in the road until the last child is safe.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A crossing guard stands by the school.

paras.label: B
paras.text: She wears a bright vest so drivers see her.

paras.label: C
paras.text: She holds up a sign that says stop.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Then she waves the children across.

paras.label: E
paras.text: She waits until every child is safe.

questions.q: Why does the crossing guard wear a bright vest?
questions.a: She wears a bright vest so every driver can see her.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the stop sign) and paragraph E (i.e. staying until the end).
Tell what a crossing guard does.
questions.a: She stands at the corner by the school in a bright vest, holds up a sign that tells cars to stop, waves the children across, and stays in the road until the last child is safe.

questions.q:
vest: a bright coat with no sleeves, worn so people can see you.
guard: a person whose job is keeping others safe.
Describe the connection between the sign and the children crossing.
questions.a: She holds up a round sign that tells cars to stop, and when the cars stop she waves the children across the street.

note: The order is the lesson here: sign first, then cars stop, then children cross. Ask what would happen if those swapped.

title: Why a Cat Purrs
standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions about key details in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A cat purrs by shaking the muscles in its throat very fast.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The shake happens when the cat breathes in and when it breathes out.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That is why a purr does not stop between breaths.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Most cats purr when they feel safe and warm.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Some cats also purr when they are hurt or scared.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A cat purrs with the muscles in its throat.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The shake happens when it breathes in and out.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So a purr does not stop between breaths.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Most cats purr when they feel safe.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Some purr when they are hurt or scared.

questions.q: What part of a cat makes the purr?
questions.a: A cat purrs by shaking the muscles in its throat very fast.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. why a purr never stops) and paragraph E (i.e. purring when hurt).
Tell how and why a cat purrs.
questions.a: A cat shakes the muscles in its throat very fast, both breathing in and breathing out, so the purr never stops between breaths. Most cats purr when they feel safe, and some purr when they are hurt or scared.

questions.q:
muscle: a part inside the body that can pull and move.
purr: the soft rumbling sound a cat makes.
Describe the connection between breathing and the sound of a purr.
questions.a: The shake happens when the cat breathes in and when it breathes out, which is why a purr does not stop between breaths.

note: Paragraph E is the surprise and children will want to talk about it. The text says some cats purr when hurt; it does not say why, and that is worth admitting.

title: The Mail Carrier's Bag
standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions about key details in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A mail carrier sorts the mail into streets before she leaves.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Each street goes in order, so the first house comes first.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Her bag is heavy at the start and light at the end.

paras.label: D
paras.text: She walks the same route every day and knows every dog.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The letters at the bottom of the bag are the last stop.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A mail carrier sorts the mail into streets.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Each street is in order, so the first house is first.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Her bag is heavy at the start.

paras.label: D
paras.text: She walks the same route every day.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The mail at the bottom is the last stop.

questions.q: What does the mail carrier do before she leaves?
questions.a: She sorts the mail into streets before she leaves.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the order) and paragraph E (i.e. the bottom of the bag).
Tell how a mail carrier gets the mail to the right houses.
questions.a: She sorts the mail into streets before she leaves, puts each street in order so the first house comes first, and walks the same route every day. The letters at the bottom of the bag are the last stop.

questions.q:
sort: to put things into groups that belong together.
route: the same path a person takes each day.
Describe the connection between sorting the mail and the bag getting lighter.
questions.a: Each street goes in order so the first house comes first, which is why her bag is heavy at the start and light at the end.

note: Children often miss that the bottom of the bag is the end of the route. It follows from paragraph B, so read those two together.

title: Bees and Flowers
standard_text:
Standard: Identify the main topic and retell key details of a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.3 connections · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A bee lands on a flower to drink the sweet nectar.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Yellow dust called pollen sticks to the hairs on her legs.

paras.label: C
paras.text: She flies to the next flower and some pollen rubs off.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That pollen helps the flower make seeds.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Bees get food and flowers get seeds, so both of them win.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A bee lands on a flower to drink.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Yellow pollen sticks to her legs.

paras.label: C
paras.text: She flies to the next flower.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Some pollen rubs off and helps make seeds.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Bees get food and flowers get seeds.

questions.q: What sticks to the bee's legs?
questions.a: Yellow dust called pollen sticks to the hairs on her legs.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the next flower) and paragraph E (i.e. both of them win).
Tell the main topic of this text.
questions.a: Bees and flowers help each other. A bee drinks nectar and pollen sticks to her legs. She rubs some off on the next flower, and that pollen helps the flower make seeds.

questions.q:
nectar: the sweet juice inside a flower.
pollen: the yellow dust a flower makes.
Describe the connection between the bee's legs and the flower's seeds.
questions.a: Pollen sticks to the hairs on her legs, and when she flies to the next flower some pollen rubs off and helps that flower make seeds.

note: The main topic is the trade, not the bee. Ask what the last paragraph adds that the first four do not.

title: The Fire Station
standard_text:
Standard: Identify the main topic and retell key details of a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.3 connections · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: The fire station is open all day and all night.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The truck is backed in so it can drive straight out.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Boots and coats wait by the truck with the pants already open.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A firefighter can step in and pull them up in seconds.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Every second saved is a second sooner at the fire.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The fire station is open all night.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The truck is backed in so it can drive out.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Boots and coats wait by the truck.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A firefighter can step in fast.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Every second saved helps.

questions.q: Why is the truck backed in?
questions.a: The truck is backed in so it can drive straight out.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the waiting boots) and paragraph E (i.e. seconds saved).
Tell the main topic of this text.
questions.a: A fire station is set up so firefighters can leave fast. The truck is backed in, the boots and coats wait by the truck with the pants open, and a firefighter can step in and pull them up in seconds.

questions.q:
station: the building where fire trucks and firefighters stay.
second: a very short piece of time.
Describe the connection between the open pants and getting to the fire.
questions.a: The pants are already open so a firefighter can step in and pull them up in seconds, and every second saved is a second sooner at the fire.

note: Everything here is one idea in five parts: be fast. Ask the child to say the idea in their own words before retelling the details.

title: How Rain Falls
standard_text:
Standard: Identify the main topic and retell key details of a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.3 connections · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: The sun warms a puddle and the water turns into vapor.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The vapor rises up into the cold air above.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Up high it cools and sticks to tiny bits of dust.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Many drops join together until they are too heavy to float.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then they fall back down as rain.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The sun warms a puddle and the water rises.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The vapor goes up into cold air.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Up high it cools into tiny drops.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Drops join until they are too heavy.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then they fall as rain.

questions.q: What makes the drops fall?
questions.a: Many drops join together until they are too heavy to float.

questions.q: Paragraph A (i.e. the sun and the puddle) and paragraph D (i.e. the drops joining).
Tell the main topic of this text.
questions.a: Water goes up and comes back down. The sun turns a puddle into vapor, the vapor rises into cold air and cools onto bits of dust, and the drops join until they are heavy enough to fall as rain.

questions.q:
vapor: water that has turned into air you cannot see.
float: to stay up without falling.
Describe the connection between the sun and the rain.
questions.a: The sun warms a puddle and the water turns into vapor, and that vapor is what rises, cools and falls back down as rain.

note: This is a circle and the text does not say so. Ask where the rain goes next, and whether paragraph A could come after paragraph E.

title: The Library Card
standard_text:
Standard: Identify the main topic and retell key details of a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.3 connections · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A library card has your name and a long number on it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The number tells the computer which books you took home.

paras.label: C
paras.text: You may keep a book for three weeks.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A card is free, and the books you borrow are free too.

paras.label: E
paras.text: When you bring a book back, someone else can read it.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A library card has your name and a number.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The number tells the computer what you took.

paras.label: C
paras.text: You may keep a book for three weeks.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The card is free and the books are free.

paras.label: E
paras.text: When you bring it back, someone else can read it.

questions.q: How long may you keep a book?
questions.a: You may keep a book for three weeks.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the number) and paragraph E (i.e. bringing a book back).
Tell the main topic of this text.
questions.a: A library card lets you borrow books for free. It has your name and a number that tells the computer which books you took, you may keep a book for three weeks, and when you bring it back someone else can read it.

questions.q:
borrow: to take something for a while and then give it back.
free: costing no money.
Describe the connection between bringing a book back and other readers.
questions.a: When you bring a book back, someone else can read it.

note: Paragraph E is the point of the whole system and it comes last. Ask why the writer saved it for the end.

title: A Seed Grows
standard_text:
Standard: Identify the main topic and retell key details of a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.3 connections · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A seed holds a tiny plant and a packed lunch for it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Water makes the hard coat swell until it cracks open.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A root goes down first, before anything goes up.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Then a green shoot pushes up toward the light.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Once the first leaves open, the plant can make its own food.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A seed holds a tiny plant and its food.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Water makes the hard coat crack open.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A root goes down first.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Then a green shoot pushes up.

paras.label: E
paras.text: When leaves open, the plant makes its own food.

questions.q: What goes out of the seed first?
questions.a: A root goes down first, before anything goes up.

questions.q: Paragraph A (i.e. the packed lunch) and paragraph E (i.e. making its own food).
Tell the main topic of this text.
questions.a: A seed grows in order. It holds a tiny plant and food for it, water cracks the coat open, a root goes down first, a shoot pushes up, and once the leaves open the plant makes its own food.

questions.q:
root: the part of a plant that grows down into the soil.
shoot: the new green stem that pushes up.
Describe the connection between the packed lunch and the first leaves.
questions.a: A seed holds a packed lunch for the tiny plant, and once the first leaves open the plant can make its own food instead.

note: Paragraph A and paragraph E are a pair: food that came with the seed, then food the plant makes. The three middle paragraphs sit between them in order.

title: The Sun and the Puddle
standard_text:
Standard: Describe the connection between two individuals, events, ideas, or pieces of information in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.8 reasons · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: On Monday the rain left a big puddle on the path.

paras.label: B
paras.text: By Tuesday the sun was out all morning.

paras.label: C
paras.text: By lunch the puddle was only a damp ring.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The sun turned the water into a vapor you cannot see.

paras.label: E
paras.text: But a puddle in the shade was still there on Wednesday.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Rain left a big puddle on the path.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The sun came out all morning.

paras.label: C
paras.text: By lunch the puddle was small.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The sun turned the water into vapor.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A puddle in the shade was still there.

questions.q: What happened to the puddle in the shade?
questions.a: A puddle in the shade was still there on Wednesday.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the sun) and paragraph E (i.e. the shade).
Tell what this text is about.
questions.a: The sun dried a puddle. Rain left a big puddle, the sun was out all morning, and by lunch it was only a damp ring. A puddle in the shade was still there the next day.

questions.q:
damp: a little bit wet.
shade: a place the sun does not reach.
Describe the connection between the sun and the puddle drying.
questions.a: The sun was out all morning and turned the water into vapor you cannot see, so by lunch the puddle was only a damp ring.

note: The shade puddle is the proof and it comes last. Ask the child what it shows that paragraphs A to D do not.

title: The Bell and the Line
standard_text:
Standard: Describe the connection between two individuals, events, ideas, or pieces of information in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.8 reasons · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: The bell rings at the end of recess every day.

paras.label: B
paras.text: When it rings, the children stop playing and walk to the line.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The line forms on the yellow paint by the door.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A teacher counts the children before the line goes in.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The bell is the start of all of it.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The bell rings at the end of recess.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The children stop playing and walk to the line.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The line forms on the yellow paint.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A teacher counts the children.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The bell starts all of it.

questions.q: Where does the line form?
questions.a: The line forms on the yellow paint by the door.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. walking to the line) and paragraph D (i.e. the counting).
Tell what happens after the bell rings.
questions.a: The bell rings at the end of recess, the children stop playing and walk to the line on the yellow paint, and a teacher counts them before the line goes in.

questions.q:
recess: the time outside for playing.
form: to come together into a shape, like a line.
Describe the connection between the bell and the children lining up.
questions.a: When the bell rings, the children stop playing and walk to the line, so the bell is the start of all of it.

note: Paragraph E names the connection outright. Cover it and see whether the child can say it before reading it.

title: Why the Beach Changes
standard_text:
Standard: Describe the connection between two individuals, events, ideas, or pieces of information in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.8 reasons · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: Early in the morning the beach is wide and flat.

paras.label: B
paras.text: By afternoon the water has come far up the sand.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The moon pulls on the ocean as the Earth turns.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That pull makes the water rise and fall twice every day.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The wide beach comes back again by night.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the morning the beach is wide.

paras.label: B
paras.text: By afternoon the water comes up the sand.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The moon pulls on the ocean.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The water rises and falls twice a day.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The wide beach comes back by night.

questions.q: How many times a day does the water rise and fall?
questions.a: That pull makes the water rise and fall twice a day.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the moon) and paragraph E (i.e. night).
Tell why the beach changes.
questions.a: The moon pulls on the ocean as the Earth turns, and that pull makes the water rise and fall twice a day. So a beach that is wide in the morning is covered by afternoon and wide again by night.

questions.q:
pull: to draw something toward you.
ocean: the very large body of salt water.
Describe the connection between the moon and the water on the sand.
questions.a: The moon pulls on the ocean as the Earth turns, and that pull makes the water rise and fall twice a day.

note: The cause is invisible and far away, which is hard at this age. Keep the child on what they can see in paragraphs A, B and E first.

title: The Farmer and the Market
standard_text:
Standard: Describe the connection between two individuals, events, ideas, or pieces of information in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.8 reasons · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A farmer picks beans early, while the air is still cool.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Cool beans stay crisp longer than warm ones do.

paras.label: C
paras.text: She packs them in boxes and drives to the market.

paras.label: D
paras.text: By eight o'clock her table is full and the doors open.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Beans picked the day before would already be soft.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A farmer picks beans early while it is cool.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Cool beans stay crisp longer than warm ones.

paras.label: C
paras.text: She packs them and drives to the market.

paras.label: D
paras.text: By eight her table is full.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Older beans would be soft.

questions.q: Why does the farmer pick beans early?
questions.a: Cool beans stay crisp longer than warm ones do.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. why cool matters) and paragraph E (i.e. older beans).
Tell why the farmer picks early.
questions.a: She picks beans early while the air is still cool, because cool beans stay crisp longer than warm ones. She packs them and drives to the market, and by eight o'clock her table is full.

questions.q:
crisp: firm and fresh, so it snaps.
market: a place where people sell food.
Describe the connection between the cool morning air and the beans on the table.
questions.a: She picks beans early while the air is still cool, because cool beans stay crisp longer than warm ones do.

note: Paragraph E is the comparison that makes the reason land. Read B and E together.

title: The Fly and the Web
standard_text:
Standard: Describe the connection between two individuals, events, ideas, or pieces of information in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.8 reasons · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A spider's web has sticky threads and plain ones mixed together.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The spider walks only on the plain threads, so it never sticks.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A fly cannot tell the two kinds apart.

paras.label: D
paras.text: When a fly hits a sticky thread, the whole web shakes.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The spider feels the shake and knows just where to go.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A web has sticky threads and plain ones.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The spider walks only on the plain ones.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A fly cannot tell them apart.

paras.label: D
paras.text: When a fly hits a sticky thread, the web shakes.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The spider feels the shake and goes there.

questions.q: Why does the spider not stick to its own web?
questions.a: The spider walks only on the plain threads, so it never sticks.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the fly not knowing) and paragraph D (i.e. the shake).
Tell how a spider knows a fly is caught.
questions.a: A web has sticky threads and plain ones mixed together, and the spider walks only on the plain ones. A fly cannot tell them apart, so when it hits a sticky thread the whole web shakes and the spider feels it.

questions.q:
thread: one thin line of a web.
plain: not sticky, just ordinary.
Describe the connection between the shaking web and the spider finding the fly.
questions.a: When a fly hits a sticky thread the whole web shakes, and the spider feels the shake and knows just where to go.

note: Two connections sit in this text: why the spider is safe, and how it gets the news. Ask the child for both.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The book says the bear will hibernate all winter long.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Hibernate is a word for a long, deep winter sleep.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A bear that hibernates does not eat for many months.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Its heart beats slower and its body stays cool.

paras.label: E
paras.text: In spring the bear wakes up thin and very hungry.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The book says the bear will hibernate all winter.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Hibernate means a long, deep winter sleep.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The bear does not eat for months.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Its heart beats slower and it stays cool.

paras.label: E
paras.text: In spring it wakes up hungry.

questions.q: What does hibernate mean?
questions.a: Hibernate is a word for a long, deep winter sleep.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. what the word means) and paragraph E (i.e. waking up).
Tell what hibernate means and what a bear does.
questions.a: Hibernate means a long, deep winter sleep. A bear that hibernates does not eat for many months, its heart beats slower and its body stays cool, and in spring it wakes up thin and very hungry.

questions.q:
hibernate: to sleep deeply all winter.
spring: the season that comes after winter.
Describe the connection between not eating and waking up thin.
questions.a: A bear that hibernates does not eat for many months, so in spring it wakes up thin and very hungry.

note: RI.1.4 is asking about a word, so paragraph B is the answer and the rest is evidence. Ask the child which paragraph gives them the meaning.

title: Words That Tell Where
standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions to help determine or clarify the meaning of words and phrases in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.5 text features · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A map uses small words to tell you where to go.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Above means higher up, and below means lower down.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Beside means right next to something else on the map.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Between means in the middle of two other things.

paras.label: E
paras.text: If you miss those small words, the map cannot help you.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A map uses small words to tell where.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Above means higher. Below means lower.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Beside means next to.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Between means in the middle of two things.

paras.label: E
paras.text: If you miss them, the map will not help.

questions.q: What does between mean?
questions.a: Between means in the middle of two other things.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. above and below) and paragraph E (i.e. missing the words).
Tell what this text teaches.
questions.a: A map uses small words to tell you where to go. Above means higher up and below means lower down, beside means right next to, and between means in the middle of two things. If you miss those words the map cannot help you.

questions.q:
beside: right next to something.
between: in the middle of two things.
Describe the connection between the small words and using a map.
questions.a: A map uses small words to tell you where to go, so if you miss those small words the map cannot help you.

note: These are the words that trip children up on every map all year. Have them put a finger on two things and say what is between them.

title: What Melt Means
standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions to help determine or clarify the meaning of words and phrases in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.5 text features · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: Melt means to change from hard into something soft and runny.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Ice melts into plain water when it gets warm enough.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Butter melts in a hot pan and spreads out flat.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A crayon left on a sunny sill can melt too.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Heat is what makes all of those things melt.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Melt means to change from hard to runny.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Ice melts into water when it is warm.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Butter melts in a hot pan.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A crayon in the sun can melt.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Heat makes all of them melt.

questions.q: What does melt mean?
questions.a: Melt means to change from hard into something soft and runny.

questions.q: Paragraph A (i.e. the meaning) and paragraph E (i.e. what they all share).
Tell what melt means and give examples.
questions.a: Melt means to change from hard into something soft and runny. Ice melts into water, butter melts in a hot pan, and a crayon on a sunny sill can melt. Heat is what makes all of those things melt.

questions.q:
melt: to change from hard into soft and runny.
heat: warmth that can change things.
Describe the connection between the three examples in the middle.
questions.a: Ice, butter and a crayon are all different, and heat is what makes all of those things melt.

note: The shape is a definition, three examples and the thing they share. Ask what all three have in common before reading paragraph E.

title: Signs at the Pool
standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions to help determine or clarify the meaning of words and phrases in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.5 text features · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A sign at the pool says NO DIVING in big letters.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Diving means going in head first instead of feet first.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Another sign says to WALK and not to run.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A third sign tells you how deep the water is.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Reading those signs before you swim keeps you safe.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A sign at the pool says NO DIVING.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Diving means going in head first.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Another sign says to walk, not run.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A third sign tells how deep the water is.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Read the signs to stay safe.

questions.q: What does diving mean?
questions.a: Diving means going in head first instead of feet first.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. what diving means) and paragraph D (i.e. the depth sign).
Tell what the signs at the pool say.
questions.a: One sign says NO DIVING, which means going in head first. Another says to walk and not run, and a third tells you how deep the water is. Reading those signs before you swim keeps you safe.

questions.q:
diving: going into water head first.
deep: going far down from the top.
Describe the connection between reading the signs and staying safe.
questions.a: Reading those signs before you swim keeps you safe.

note: The word children get wrong is diving, because they use it for any jump. Paragraph B is there for exactly that.

title: Float and Sink
standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions to help determine or clarify the meaning of words and phrases in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.5 text features · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: Float means to stay up on top of the water.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Sink means to go all the way down to the bottom.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A cork floats, and a small rock sinks.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A big boat floats even though it is very heavy.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So what matters is not just weight but shape too.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Float means to stay on top of the water.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Sink means to go down to the bottom.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A cork floats and a rock sinks.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A big boat floats, and it is heavy.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So weight is not the only thing.

questions.q: What does sink mean?
questions.a: Sink means to go all the way down to the bottom.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the cork and the rock) and paragraph D (i.e. the boat).
Tell what float and sink mean.
questions.a: Float means to stay up on top of the water and sink means to go down to the bottom. A cork floats and a small rock sinks, but a big heavy boat floats too, so what matters is not just weight but shape.

questions.q:
float: to stay up on top of water.
sink: to go down to the bottom.
Describe the connection between the boat and the rest of the text.
questions.a: A cork floats and a small rock sinks, but a big boat floats even though it is very heavy, so what matters is not just weight but shape too.

note: Paragraph D breaks the rule paragraph C sets up, and that is deliberate. Ask the child why a heavy boat does not sink.

standard_text:

 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: The first page of this book is a list.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The list shows every part of the book in order.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Next to each part is the page it starts on.

paras.label: D
paras.text: If you want frogs, the list sends you to page nine.

paras.label: E
paras.text: You do not have to turn every page to find it.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The first page of this book is a list.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It shows every part in order.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Each part has a page number.

paras.label: D
paras.text: If you want frogs, go to page nine.

paras.label: E
paras.text: You do not turn every page.

questions.q: What is next to each part on the list?
questions.a: Next to each part is the page it starts on.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. finding frogs) and paragraph E (i.e. not turning every page).
Tell what the list at the front is for.
questions.a: The first page is a list that shows every part of the book in order, with the page each part starts on. If you want frogs the list sends you to page nine, so you do not have to turn every page.

questions.q:
list: names written one under another.
page number: the number that tells you which page you are on.
Describe the connection between the list and finding what you want.
questions.a: Next to each part is the page it starts on, so the list sends you straight to page nine instead of turning every page.

note: This is a table of contents and the text never uses the term. Name it after the child has used it, not before.

paras.label: A
paras.text: At the back of the book there is a word list.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It holds the hard words from every page.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The words are in ABC order, so they are easy to find.

paras.label: D
paras.text: After each word is a short line that tells what it means.

paras.label: E
paras.text: You can look up a word without asking anyone.

paras.label: A
paras.text: At the back of the book is a word list.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It holds the hard words.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The words are in ABC order.

paras.label: D
paras.text: After each word is what it means.

paras.label: E
paras.text: You can look up a word by yourself.

questions.q: What order are the words in?
questions.a: The words are in ABC order, so they are easy to find.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. ABC order) and paragraph E (i.e. looking it up yourself).
Tell what the word list at the back is for.
questions.a: The back of the book has a list of the hard words from every page, in ABC order, with a short line after each one telling what it means. You can look up a word without asking anyone.

questions.q:
ABC order: the order of the letters of the alphabet.
means: what a word is telling you.
Describe the connection between ABC order and finding a word fast.
questions.a: The words are in ABC order, so they are easy to find and you can look one up without asking anyone.

note: This is a glossary. Point out that it only holds words from this book, which is what makes it different from a dictionary.

title: Headings Tell You Where
standard_text:
Standard: Know and use various text features, such as headings, a table of contents, a glossary and icons, to locate key facts or information in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.6 pictures and words · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A heading is the dark line above a part of a page.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It says in a few words what that part is about.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A heading that says Eggs tells you eggs come next.

paras.label: D
paras.text: You can read just the headings to find what you need.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Headings save you from reading the whole page.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A heading is the dark line above a part.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It tells what that part is about.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A heading that says Eggs means eggs come next.

paras.label: D
paras.text: You can read just the headings.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Headings save you reading the whole page.

questions.q: What does a heading tell you?
questions.a: It says in a few words what that part is about.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the Eggs heading) and paragraph E (i.e. saving reading).
Tell what headings do.
questions.a: A heading is the dark line above a part of a page, and it says in a few words what that part is about. A heading that says Eggs tells you eggs come next, so you can read just the headings to find what you need.

questions.q:
heading: the dark line of words above a part of a page.
about: what something is telling you.
Describe the connection between reading headings and reading the whole page.
questions.a: You can read just the headings to find what you need, which saves you from reading the whole page.

note: Have the child find a heading in any book on the shelf and say what will come under it before they read it.

title: Buttons You Can Tap
standard_text:
Standard: Know and use various text features, such as headings, a table of contents, a glossary and icons, to locate key facts or information in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.6 pictures and words · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A screen has small pictures you can tap with a finger.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A tiny house always takes you back to the start.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A round glass means you can search for something.

paras.label: D
paras.text: An arrow that curls back means undo what you just did.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The pictures mean the same thing on almost every screen.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A screen has small pictures you can tap.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A tiny house takes you back to the start.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A round glass means you can search.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A curled arrow means undo.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The pictures mean the same on most screens.

questions.q: What does the tiny house do?
questions.a: A tiny house always takes you back to the start.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the curling arrow) and paragraph E (i.e. every screen).
Tell what the small pictures on a screen do.
questions.a: A screen has small pictures you tap with a finger. A tiny house takes you back to the start, a round glass means search, and an arrow that curls back means undo. They mean the same thing on almost every screen.

questions.q:
tap: to touch a screen once with a finger.
undo: to take back what you just did.
Describe the connection between learning these pictures and using a new screen.
questions.a: The pictures mean the same thing on almost every screen, so learning them once helps on a screen you have never used.

note: Paragraph E is the useful part and children will skip it for the pictures. It is why learning three icons is worth the time.

title: The Numbers at the Bottom
standard_text:
Standard: Know and use various text features, such as headings, a table of contents, a glossary and icons, to locate key facts or information in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.6 pictures and words · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: Look at the very bottom corner of this page.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A small number sits there, and the next page is one more.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Page numbers let a list at the front point at a page.

paras.label: D
paras.text: They also let you stop reading and find your place again.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A book with no page numbers is hard to talk about.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Look at the bottom corner of the page.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A small number sits there.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The next page is one more.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Numbers help you find your place again.

paras.label: E
paras.text: They also let the list point at a page.

questions.q: Where do you find the page number?
questions.a: Look at the very bottom corner of this page.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. pointing from the list) and paragraph D (i.e. finding your place).
Tell what page numbers are for.
questions.a: A small number sits at the bottom corner of each page, and the next page is one more. Page numbers let the list at the front point at a page, and they let you stop reading and find your place again.

questions.q:
corner: the spot where two edges of a page meet.
place: the spot you stopped at.
Describe the connection between page numbers and the list at the front.
questions.a: Page numbers let a list at the front point at a page.

note: Best done with a real book open. Ask the child to find page nine two ways: by turning, and by using the list.
